title.narrative: NARRATIVE REPORT OF THE YEAR 1 ON SCHOOL ANTI-TRAFFICKING EDUCATION AND ADVOCACY PROJECT (STEAP)

description.narrative: EXECUTIVE SUMMARYThe School Anti-Trafficking Education and Advocacy Project (STEAP) is a flagship initiative designed to tackle human trafficking in Nigeria by safeguarding school-aged children and building resilient education systems. Funded by the Government of the Netherlands and implemented by the International Centre for Migration Policy Development (ICMPD), STEAP focuses on five high-risk states—Benue, Delta, Edo, Enugu, and Ogun—identified as trafficking hotspots due to recurring incidents of child exploitation and systemic vulnerabilities.The primary aim of STEAP is to strengthen awareness, enhance stakeholder capacity, foster collaborations with Civil Society Organizations (CSOs), and help create a conducive environment for the prevention of human trafficking amongst school age children before it occurs. The project goes beyond conventional awareness campaigns by integrating anti-trafficking education into teacher training curricula, supporting the formation of school-based anti-trafficking vanguard clubs, and developing evidence-based tools and systems for long-term prevention and accountability.Key achievements during the first year of implementation (December 2023 – November 2024) include:1.Institutional and stakeholder engagement-Official project launch held in Abuja in February 2024.-Advocacy visits conducted to Commissioners of Education and Attorneys General across all five states.-All five states pledged support and provided in-kind office accommodations for project teams.-The 250 schools for the inauguration of anti-trafficking vanguards selected-Appointment of Desk Officers in each State Ministry of Education to serve as focal points for project coordination and monitoring in 250 selected schools (50 per state).2.Evidence-based design and baseline assessment-A comprehensive baseline survey was conducted, combining surveys, interviews, and focus group discussions across the five states.-The baseline findings were validated by 292 key stakeholders (143 males, 149 females), including representatives from NAPTIP, Ministries of Education and Justice, CSOs, School-Based Management Committees (SBMCs), and religious/community leaders.-Key gaps identified included low awareness of trafficking among students and teachers, lack of standardized reporting tools, and weak coordination between schools and protection services.3.Capacity building and curriculum integration.-85 lecturers and tutors (19 per state) from 38 Colleges of Education were trained through a 3-day Training-of-Trainers (ToT) workshop on the National Commission for Colleges of Education (NCCE) developed THB curriculum for teacher training-Post-training assessments demonstrated significant improvement in participants' understanding and readiness to roll out the curriculum within their institutions.-The participants for the ToTs have since developed and submitted action plans to cascade the training to peers across their respective states.4.Civil society engagement and community mobilization-Five (5) CSOs—one per state—were selected following a rigorous vetting and due diligence process in partnership with the Network Against Child Trafficking, Abuse and Labour (NACTAL).-These CSOs were trained and are now positioned to support community outreach, sensitization, and local awareness activities planned for Year 2 (2025).5.Development and review of reporting tools, SOPs and other systems in partnership with NAPTIP, the project developed and validated:-Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) for establishing and running school-based anti-trafficking vanguard clubs.-Revised reporting tools and information, education and communication (IEC) materials tailored for school settings.-A Vanguard Club Handbook to guide student-led anti-trafficking action in the 250 selected schools.6.Strategic coordination at the state level-Desk officers serve as the official liaison between the Ministries of Education and the STEAP team.-Their responsibilities include coordinating school-level engagement, facilitating communication with key stakeholders (e.g., school principals, SBMCs, community leaders), resolving operational challenges, and ensuring fidelity to project standards.Despite achieving notable progress in 2024, the STEAP project faced delays in implementing several key activities planned for the reporting period due to a late project start, staffing transitions, and coordination challenges with government and community stakeholders. As a result, essential interventions ranging from CSO led community outreach and teacher training to the establishment and capacity-building of School-Based Management Committees (SBMCs), and the development of trafficking reporting systems were postponed. These activities have now been strategically rescheduled for 2025, where they will be implemented with improved alignment, stronger coordination, and greater stakeholder involvement. Their execution is critical to advancing the project’s goals of community engagement, institutional capacity strengthening, and system development for trafficking prevention. Integrated into the 2025 work plan, these deferred activities will not only help realise the intended outcomes but also reinforce the project’s sustainability and long-term impact.Overall, in its first year of implementation, STEAP has laid a solid foundation through strategic partnerships with key stakeholders, institutional capacity-building, and evidence-based programming. In 2025, the next phase of the project will focus on inaugurating School Anti-Trafficking Vanguard Clubs and related activities, rolling out community outreach and awareness initiatives led by CSOs, establishing clear reporting lines and referral pathways, and further strengthening coordination between schools, SBMCs, and their surrounding communities amongst others.STEAP NARRATIVE THEORY OF CHANGE (TOC) The STEAP project is premised on the belief that if schools and communities are equipped with the right knowledge, structures, and partnerships, they can become active agents in preventing and responding to child trafficking. The project targets trafficking hotspots in Nigeria where school-aged children are particularly vulnerable due to poverty, low awareness, and weak protective institutions.The ToC assumes that:i.Awareness is a powerful preventive tool—when children, teachers, and parents are informed, they are less likely to fall victim to trafficking.ii.Schools can act as hubs for early detection and reporting if they are given the tools and connections to do so.iii.Collaboration between schools, CSOs, and government institutions leads to more coordinated prevention, referral, and survivor support systems.Therefore, STEAP will:i.Integrate anti-trafficking education into teacher training institutions.ii.Establish school-based anti-trafficking vanguard clubs and safe reporting mechanisms.iii.Train CSOs and state actors to increase their technical capacity in prevention and victim protection.iv.Build strong, formalized linkages between education authorities and law enforcement.By doing this, the project will contribute to:•Reducing the incidence of child trafficking in targeted states.•Creating school environments that are safe and protective.•Strengthening the capacity of frontline actors to detect, refer, and support victims.•Empowering students and educators to act against THB within their communities.Ultimately, the STEAP project aims to foster a cultural shift—where trafficking is recognized early, challenged collectively, and survivors are supported with dignity.STRATEGIC PURPOSEThe STEAP project was strategically designed to respond to the urgent challenge of THB, particularly as it affects school-aged children in Nigeria’s trafficking hotspots. The project focuses on reducing vulnerabilities caused by limited awareness, weak protective structures within schools and communities, cultural indifference toward child exploitation, and inadequate support systems for survivors.STEAP is grounded in a Theory of Change that emphasizes prevention through education, early detection through community engagement, and protection through institutional coordination. The initiative takes a holistic approach, targeting not just students, but the entire school ecosystem including teachers, parents, SBMCs, and CSOs.Core strategies include:•Establishing student-led anti-trafficking school clubs (vanguards) selected schools which are in high-risk areas •Enhancing the capacity of school personnel and frontline stakeholders to identify and report suspected cases•Building strong reporting systems for survivors; and referral pathways for victims•Fostering partnerships between education authorities, NAPTIP, CSOs, and relevant stakeholders.The project design reflects insights gathered through extensive consultations with key stakeholders, including NAPTIP, the Federal Ministry of Education, State Ministries of Education, and experienced anti-trafficking NGOs. These consultations shaped the ‘whole of school community’ model, ensuring that the approach addresses both the root causes and symptoms of trafficking.STEAP's overarching goal is to build a protective environment around school-aged children by:•Strengthening awareness on trafficking risks and response strategies.•Enhancing technical and institutional capacities of stakeholders to combat THB.•Fostering collaboration with CSO and survivor-centred reintegration.•Supporting multi-stakeholder action and alignment with national child protection frameworks.Specific objectives:•Raise awareness among secondary school students, parents, and teachers on the dangers of trafficking, and equip them with practical skills to prevent, detect, and safely respond to potential incidents.•Strengthen the technical capacities of schools, school clubs, and government and civil society stakeholders to identify, report, and respond to trafficking threats—while supporting localized, sustainable interventions.•Facilitate the protection and reintegration of trafficking survivors into the education system, with provision of psychosocial support in collaboration with CSOs.•Strengthen linkages between schools and law enforcement agencies, enabling timely identification and referral of student-related trafficking or exploitation cases.NEW DEVELOPMENTS IN TRAFFICKING IN NIGERIADuring the reporting period, the landscape of human trafficking in Nigeria witnessed the emergence of disturbing new trends that challenge conventional prevention approaches. These developments demand adaptive responses and reinforced community engagement strategies:•Sextortion as a control mechanism: A growing number of trafficking networks are now using sextortion—the coercion of victims into sending sexually explicit images or videos, which are then used to blackmail or control them. This digital abuse is increasingly prevalent among school-aged girls who are approached online.•Cross-border cybercrime exploitation: Young boys are being recruited under false pretences and trafficked to neighbouring countries—especially Ghana—to engage in internet fraud (“Yahoo Yahoo”). When these boys fail to meet daily fraud targets, they are subjected to maltreatment, confinement, or even physical abuse.•Trafficking for Egg harvesting: With the proliferation of In-Vitro Fertilization (IVF) clinics in Nigeria, a new pattern of exploitation has surfaced. Vulnerable adolescent girls are reportedly being lured, medicated, and subjected to hormonal treatments to stimulate egg production. These eggs are then harvested and sold to fertility centres, often without informed consent or medical oversight.In response to these evolving threats, STEAP project has scaled up and planned more of its awareness creation efforts through a multi-platform approach:•Online: Targeted campaigns addressing digital grooming and sextortion.•Traditional Media: Radio discussions and community outreach in local languages.•Community engagements: Townhall meetings, school-based discussions, and public gatherings to sensitize parents, teachers, religious and community leaders.A powerful example of local leadership making an impact is the intervention by the Oba of Benin in Edo State. His continued public condemnation and spiritual sanctions on traditional priests who administer oaths to trafficked victims in Edo State has significantly contributed to a reported decline in trafficking activities in the region. These experiences underscore a critical lesson for anti-trafficking interventions, that – ‘sustainable prevention is achievable when cultural, community, and institutional leaders unite to reject trafficking in all its forms’. STEAP project remains committed to continually leveraging these local partnerships as it adapts to new and emerging threats within and around its operating context.¬¬¬¬¬¬¬¬¬¬¬¬¬¬¬KEY STRATEGIC PARTNERSHIPSDuring the first year of implementation, the STEAP project strategically strengthened partnerships across national and subnational levels to enhance the sustainability and effectiveness of anti-trafficking interventions targeting school-aged children.At the national level, ICMPD continued to collaborate closely with the National Agency for the Prohibition of Trafficking in Persons (NAPTIP), a key government institution mandated to coordinate anti-trafficking efforts in Nigeria. This partnership has been instrumental in co-developing technical tools, SOPs, reporting templates, and IEC materials for use in schools and communities throughout the project locations. NAPTIP’s technical leadership also ensured alignment with national frameworks and facilitated access to State Task Forces and frontline law enforcement actors on human trafficking.In parallel, ICMPD partnered with the NCCE to train tutors from the colleges of Education on the NCCE developed and approved THB curriculum for pre-service training of teachers. Through this collaboration, a Training-of-Trainers (ToT) programme was successfully rolled out, targeting 99 lecturers from 38 public and private Colleges of Education across Benue, Delta, Edo, Enugu, and Ogun states. These trainers were equipped with the content and methodologies required to deliver the developed THB curriculum for pre-service teacher training thereby institutionalizing trafficking prevention in Nigeria’s teacher education pipeline.At the state level, STEAP secured commitments from State Ministries of Education and Justice, who not only pledged political support but also facilitated access to schools and provided operational support such as dedicated office spaces for state project teams. Desk Officers were officially designated by each State Ministry of Education to serve as focal points for implementation and coordination across the 250 selected schools.Additionally, the project partnered with NACTAL to identify and assess community-based CSOs with capacity to support local community outreach and awareness activities. Five CSOs (one per state) were ultimately selected to serve as key actors in community sensitization, capacity building for members of the SBMC, and survivor reintegration support.These multi-level partnerships have laid a strong foundation for STEAP’s long-term impact and have been crucial in ensuring local ownership, alignment with government policies, and readiness for the next phase of community-based implementation. DESCRIPTION OF STEAP ACTIVITIES BY RESULTS AREAResult 1.1: A comprehensive assessment of the state school system, stakeholder capacity and mapping of anti-trafficking projects in each state is conducted.Activity 1.1.1: Baseline assessment, training needs assessment, and mapping of existing anti-trafficking projects.During the reporting period and as a foundational step in the STEAP project, a comprehensive baseline assessment was conducted and successfully validated across the five implementing states—Benue, Delta, Edo, Enugu, and Ogun. The assessment aimed to establish the current state of awareness, institutional capacity, and community readiness to address THB within school environments. The baseline employed a robust mixed-methods approach to generate both quantitative data and qualitative insights. Key methodologies included:•Surveys: Administered to a representative sample of students, teachers, parents, and community members to assess general knowledge, perceptions, and attitudes toward human trafficking.•Key Informant Interviews (KIIs): Conducted with education officials, CSO representatives, law enforcement personnel, and other key stakeholders to explore structural gaps and opportunities.•Focus Group Discussions (FGDs): Organized with demographic groups—youth, teachers, community leaders—to understand local vulnerabilities, cultural practices, and community-level dynamics around THB.The assessment highlighted both opportunities and challenges in advancing school-based anti-trafficking interventions, and the opportunities include:a.Existing networks (e.g., SBMCs, PTAs) are strong and willing to support THB prevention.b.A fair degree of political will exists among education and justice sector leaders.c.Schools serve as a trusted platform for community-level engagement and awareness.While the challenges are:•Low baseline awareness of THB indicators among students and teachers.•Inconsistent or non-existent reporting and referral mechanisms in schools.•Limited capacity of teachers and CSOs to deliver trafficking-related education.•Lack of culturally and gender-sensitive materials and interventions.•Variability in engagement between urban and rural communities.The baseline report thus recommends a multi-pronged response which further expanded the STEAP project approach:1)Localize the THB education content to reflect the cultural context of each community.2)Build stronger school-community linkages to support early warning systems.3)Integrate gender-sensitive approaches to address the unique vulnerabilities of girls (e.g., sextortion, egg harvesting) and boys (e.g., online recruitment for cyber scams).4)Expand training programs for teachers, school administrators, and CSO partners.5)Standardize referral pathways and ensure teachers and students know how and where to report cases safely.SUMMARY OF BASELINE ASSESSMENT FINDINGS BY STEAP RESULTS AREASRESULT AREA 1: Raise awareness among school communities about the dangers of THBKey findings:•Students in Delta had the highest awareness of THB strategies (up to 86% aware of promises to parents), but only 4–5% knew someone affected—suggesting high awareness is linked to lower exposure.•Benue students had lower awareness (e.g., 62% aware of recruitment by paying parents), but higher exposure—30% knew victims and 33% knew children living in cramped, poor conditions.•Awareness of danger signs was lowest in Ogun (e.g., only 28% aware of deception around education; 40% aware of housing conditions as a sign of trafficking).•At least 1 in 3 students in each state reported knowing of children taken away to repay loans.Adaptation strategy:•In Benue and Enugu: STEAP will increase multimedia sensitization to bridge the awareness–exposure gap.•In Ogun: STEAP will prioritize school-wide awareness campaigns targeting low-recognition of danger signs.•In Delta: STEAP will focus on sustainability by involving students in peer-led education and tracking improvements.RESULT AREA 2: Strengthen technical capacities of schools, school clubs, and stakeholdersKey findings:•83% of students reported receiving some THB information in schools, but most via general subjects—not specialized content.•No schools in Delta or Ogun engaged parents via PTAs on trafficking topics.•Teachers across all states showed limited capacity to identify complex trafficking signs.•CSOs and school staff expressed demand for training and SOPs.Adaptation strategy:•STEAP will roll out specialized training of teachers with state-customized modules based on identified weak areas (e.g., Ogun on THB signs; Edo on gendered vulnerabilities).•STEAP will support the incorporation of anti-THB content into extracurricular and PTA meetings (especially in Delta and Ogun).•STEAP will support the NAPTIP to formalize school vanguard clubs in all 250 schools with training kits and SOPs as core tools.RESULT AREA 3: Protect victims, support reintegration, and collaborate with CSOsKey findings:•Benue had the highest number of students who knew victims of abuse or isolation from families.•Enugu and Edo students reported unaccompanied movement and “juju oaths” as part of trafficking.•Across all states, students highlighted that trafficked peers often lacked access to schooling or were deceived about education opportunities.•Existing referral structures in schools were inconsistent or absent.Adaptation strategy:•STEAP will establish referral pathways starting with 10 model schools per state and progressively expand.•STEAP will link CSOs to schools in Benue and Edo to identify vulnerable returnee children and provide psychosocial support.•STEAP will use PTA forums to normalize conversations about reintegration and stigma reduction.RESULT AREA 4: Strengthen collaboration with law enforcement and other institutionsKey findings:1.Multiple forms of recruitment identified (e.g., “economic promises,” peer recruitment, religious deception).2.Delta and Edo showed the greatest presence of structured trafficking networks using peer recruiters.3.Reporting is unstandardized across all states; some parents confirmed giving children to agents “in trust.”Adaptation strategy:•STEAP will work with State task forces and security agencies per LGA and introduce them to school communities.•Establish state-level THB ‘Response Working Groups’ (Ministry of Education, NAPTIP, Police, SBMCs, CSOs).•Pilot a standardized reporting tool in 2 LGAs per state for school–CSO–government coordination.Activity1.1.2: Validate the findings of project baseline assessments in a stakeholders’ workshop.Baseline implementation and validationThe survey was led by an expert in THB, child protection, and education systems, supported by trained enumerators from NACTAL across all five states. Following data collection and analysis, a series of validation workshops were conducted in each state, reaching a total of 292 participants (143 males, 149 females). Stakeholders represented at the baseline validation included:1.NAPTIP2.Ministries of Education and Justice from STEAP implementing states3.CSOs and State task forces on TIP4.SBMC and PTA members5.Traditional and religious leadersThe workshops served as a platform to validate findings, correct discrepancies, update data, and secure local ownership of the baseline report. Each state formally endorsed the report for use as a program reference document moving forward.Result 1.2: Teachers are trained on the topic of THB and successfully transmit this knowledge to their students.Activity 1.2.1: Training of trainers: Train teacher-trainers using FME approved curriculum infused with trafficking concepts.During the reporting period and as part of STEAP’s collaboration with the National Commission for Colleges of Education (NCCE), and in line with STEAP’s mandate to strengthen teaching capacity on Trafficking in Human Beings (THB), STEAP rolled out two (2) clusters of Training-of-Trainers (ToT) workshops targeting tutors from colleges of education, , Ministry of Education officials, and representatives from NAPTIP, the National Orientation Agency (NOA), and child protection units. These sessions served as a core component of STEAP’s strategy to decentralize anti-trafficking knowledge and interventions, building localized capacity to detect, prevent, and respond to trafficking in persons (TIP), especially among school-aged children across the five implementing states: Benue, Delta, Edo, Enugu, and Ogun.The workshops were designed using a participatory approach and structured around NAPTIP & NCCE Anti-Trafficking Training Manual on the THB curriculum, which was tailored for the Nigerian school and community context. Training modules covered the definition and typologies of TIP, early warning signs, national legal and policy frameworks, survivor referral pathways, gender-sensitive and trauma-informed practices, and effective community engagement strategies. Interactive sessions employed storytelling, role-play, and real-life case studies to foster participant comprehension and adaptability to their local realities. In addition to enhancing participant knowledge, the ToT workshops were instrumental in launching cascade training plans in each state, aimed at reaching over 1,500 secondary beneficiaries in five states, including students, teachers, parents, and traditional gatekeepers. Participants developed detailed action plans after the tot to step down the training. Furthermore, 85 printed training manuals and complementary visual aids including referral guides, posters, and reporting templates—were distributed to support replication efforts. These steps are expected to create a ripple effect, institutionalizing anti-trafficking awareness within the school system and beyond.Overall, the ToT workshops have not only enhanced the capacity of frontline stakeholders but have also catalysed state-level coordination and ownership, advancing STEAP’s mission to combat trafficking in persons through education and community engagement.Why the ToT? Because we know that to reach the classroom, we have to start with the teacher-trainers. That’s why we didn’t just hand over the curriculum we brought tutors into the room, equipped them with the tools, and worked with them on how to deliver this content in real-world classroom settings. Between the 2- clustered workshops, STEAP trained a total of 99 tutors drawn from 38 colleges (both public and private). These tutors are now primed to integrate the developed THB curriculum into their teacher education programs. The focus was not just content—but delivery. Sessions covered key trafficking concepts, interactive teaching methods, gender-sensitive engagement, and community-based risk narratives.The impact of the training was not only observed, but it was also measured. Pre- and post-training assessments revealed a consistent and significant improvement in participant knowledge, with an average increase of 35–40% across all participating states. This measurable gain affirmed the effectiveness of the workshops in equipping participants with a deeper understanding of how trafficking affects schoolchildren and how prevention strategies can be integrated into everyday pedagogy. Facilitators reported increased confidence in identifying trafficking risks and delivering sensitization sessions within school and community settings. To ensure sustainability, each state team developed a concrete step-down plan, detailing how the 99 trained facilitators will replicate the training across their local institutions. To support this rollout, participants received comprehensive starter kits including teaching slides, case studies, referral templates, and session guides.CASE STORY “I’ve been teaching civic education for 11 years, but this is the first time I realized how trafficking can start in the classroom—through a girl being promised a scholarship, or a boy being lured to another state for ‘IT jobs’. This training opened my eyes. I’ve already scheduled a session with my department to begin integration by next semester.”— Mr. Adebayo, Lecturer, Ogun State College of EducationResult 2.2: State and local government officials connected to the welfare of youths (incl. ministries of sports, youth, health, education, State Task Forces, law enforcement agencies, etc.) have upgraded capacities and possess up to date knowledge on THB.Activity 2.2.2: Training workshops for State Task Forces, LGEAs, and ministries of sports, youth, health, education, law enforcement agencies, and NAPTIP at State level to strengthen their capacities.In October 2024, the STEAP project convened a strategic training and sensitization workshop in Asaba, Delta State, targeting key stakeholders in the education sector. Participants included representatives from the Federal Ministry of Education (FME), Local Government Education Authorities (LGEAs), and other relevant educational institutions and agencies. This engagement was a critical component of the project’ success, designed to ensure that stakeholders at all levels are properly informed and aligned with the objectives, scope, and implementation strategy of the School Anti-Trafficking Education and Advocacy Project (STEAP).Recognizing that stakeholder buy in and institutional awareness are essential for the sustainability of project outcomes, the training aimed to familiarize participants with the broader context of Trafficking in Human Beings (THB), introduce them to the STEAP intervention model, and provide a detailed overview of the activities to implemented. The workshop also emphasized the importance of multi-level collaboration and the central role that education stakeholders at all level play in supporting school-based prevention and community sensitization.A total of 67 participants (40 male, 27 female) were trained during the workshop. The sessions focused on the forms, drivers, and impacts of human trafficking in Nigeria, with a particular emphasis on the vulnerabilities of school-aged children. Participants were also guided through the content and structure of the newly approved THB curriculum for Colleges of Education, including proposed classroom methodologies, referral pathways, and gender-sensitive approaches to child protection.The engagement was well received, with participants expressing appreciation for being included early in the implementation process. Many acknowledged that the training equipped them with accurate information and a unified narrative about STEAP, which would enable them to support and promote the project within their respective agencies. By the end of the workshop, participants pledged their commitment to the success of STEAP, noting that early involvement had enhanced their understanding of their roles and responsibilities in facilitating effective implementation.This foundational activity not only strengthened institutional ownership of STEAP but also laid the groundwork for coordinated action between federal, state, and local education actors. The outcomes of the training are expected to contribute significantly to the smooth rollout of subsequent activities, including school-level sensitization, teacher capacity-building, and other project related activities.Result 2.3: Relevant CSOs have upgraded capacities for the fight against THB.Activity 2.3.1: Identify suitable non-profit organizations working on THB to collaborate with the project.As part of efforts to deepen community engagement and ensure localized implementation of the School Anti-Trafficking Education and Advocacy Project (STEAP), the project team undertook a comprehensive process to identify and onboard qualified Civil Society Organizations (CSOs) across the five target states of Benue, Delta, Edo, Enugu, and Ogun. This initiative aligns with STEAP’s strategic objective to strengthen multi-actor collaboration at the grassroots level, particularly in raising awareness, supporting school-based sensitization, and facilitating early detection and referral of trafficking in persons (TIP) cases.In April 2024, the project team received a list of vetted and active anti-trafficking CSOs from the Network Against Trafficking, Abuse, and Labour (NACTAL). This list served as the foundation for initial outreach and potential partnership consideration. To standardize the selection process and ensure transparency, ICMPD developed and shared a structured screening checklist and application form with all nominated CSOs. The form required organizations to provide details on their governance structure, operational footprint, experience with TIP or child protection programming, presence in the target state, staff capacity, and previous donor-funded project experience. CSOs were also asked to submit supporting documents such as registration certificates, financial statements, project references, and staff resumes.Upon receiving completed submissions, ICMPD conducted an internal desk review, using pre-defined criteria to assess organizational eligibility, relevance to project goals, and implementation capacity. This review led to the shortlisting of 2 to 3 CSOs per state. To verify submitted claims and further assess suitability, the project team conducted physical due diligence visits to each of the pre-selected CSOs between May and June 2024. These field visits involved structured interviews with organizational leadership, inspection of physical infrastructure (e.g., office space, documentation systems), review of past program records, and evaluation of human resource and financial management systems. Particular attention was paid to the CSOs’ existing networks with schools, SBMCs, community leaders, and local government agencies factors considered critical for effective STEAP delivery.Following the completion of due diligence, one CSO per state was selected, resulting in a total of five (5) CSOs being formally onboarded to support project implementation. The final selection was further validated through the administration of ICMPD’s Organizational Capacity Assessment Tool (OCAT), which evaluated each organization's internal systems, operational maturity, governance practices, risk management protocols, and readiness to implement donor-funded activities. Selection decisions were guided by a balanced scoring system, with clear thresholds for programmatic, operational, and compliance capabilities. The selected CSOs demonstrated strong community presence, thematic expertise in trafficking or child protection, and an ability to mobilize local actors in support of the STEAP goals.These CSOs have been contracted for a 12-month implementation period, during which they will support school and community outreach, coordination with SBMCs, monitoring of cascade trainings, and community-based referrals. To prepare them for this role, a dedicated capacity-building and onboarding workshop has been scheduled for the first quarter of 2025. This training will cover the STEAP project framework, anti-trafficking content, child protection principles, ethical programming standards, community mobilization techniques, and ICMPD’s financial and programmatic reporting requirements. The workshop will also introduce CSOs to the tools for monitoring their field activities, managing risks, and documenting lessons learned for ongoing learning and adaptation.Through this CSO engagement process, the project reinforces its commitment to inclusive, community-driven implementation, while ensuring that local actors are equipped with the technical, operational, and coordination capacities needed to sustainably prevent trafficking in persons across STEAP's five focus states. This approach supports broader outcomes under the project’s results matrix—specifically the achievement of Output 1.2 (Local partnerships established and strengthened for TIP prevention and response) and Output 1.4 (Community actors mobilized to support school-based anti-trafficking efforts).ACTIVITIES PLANNED FOR YEAR 1 (2024) BUT NOT IMPLEMENTEDDespite notable progress and key achievements in 2024, the STEAP project encountered a few delays that prevented the full implementation of all planned activities within the reporting period. These delays were primarily the result of a later-than-anticipated project start-up, staffing transitions, and coordination challenges with both government and community stakeholders. As a result, several activities have been rescheduled for implementation in 2025. These activities remain central to the project’s outcomes and are now strategically positioned within the upcoming 2025 year’s work plan to ensure greater coherence, stakeholder ownership, and long-term impact. Below is a summary of the deferred activities, along with the rationale for their postponement:•Community outreach and training by Civil Society Organisations (CSOs) - This activity was delayed due to extended onboarding and contracting processes with selected implementing CSOs. Given the central role these CSOs will play in facilitating community engagement and driving behaviour change at the grassroots level, this activity has been prioritized for rollout in mid-2025. Strengthened onboarding processes will ensure that CSOs are better equipped and aligned with project goals, thereby improving the quality and sustainability of outreach interventions.•Training of classroom and head teachers - This activity was strategically deferred to allow for the approval of THB infused curricula by FME, as well as alignment with the academic calendar to maximise participation and relevance. This training is a cornerstone of the project’s education and prevention outcomes, as it equips educators with the knowledge and tools needed to identify and respond to trafficking risks and related vulnerabilities within school environments.•Collection of ideas from School-Based Management Committees (SBMCs) on community awareness - Originally planned as a standalone activity, this engagement has been rescheduled to coincide with the SBMC assessment on trafficking in human beings (THB) issues. The delay, largely tied to CSO onboarding timelines, now presents an opportunity to gather richer, more informed input from SBMCs, strengthening community-driven strategies for awareness and prevention.•Training-of-Trainers (ToT) for CSOs on THB prevention and response - This critical capacity-building activity has been strategically incorporated into the broader CSO onboarding and training process scheduled for 2025. By integrating it into the initial training phase, CSOs will be better positioned to lead evidence-based and survivor-sensitive programming from the outset, enhancing the overall quality of community-level interventions.•Support for the establishment of SBMCs in project schools - The formation and revitalisation of SBMCs was delayed due to the knock-on effects of CSO onboarding timelines. However, consultations with school and community stakeholders are currently underway, and this foundational activity is set to proceed in early 2025. SBMCs are essential for promoting school accountability and enabling sustained local ownership of anti-trafficking efforts.•Capacity-building training for SBMCs - Postponed until after SBMCs are formally established, this activity will now be informed by the results of the upcoming SBMC assessments. This approach ensures that training is not only well-timed but also responsive to the specific strengths and gaps identified within each SBMC, thereby enhancing their effectiveness as key actors in school governance and child protection.•Development of school priorities and identification of school improvement projects - This activity is intrinsically linked to meaningful SBMC engagement. It has been rescheduled for Quarter 2 of 2025 to follow the full activation of SBMCs. The process is designed to empower school representatives in collaboration with members of the SBMCs to articulate and address their most pressing needs, thereby reinforcing community ownership.•Design of a THB reporting system with State Taskforces - While progress has been made through ongoing dialogue with State Ministries of Education and Justice as well as the NAPTIP and state taskforces, full implementation will take place in 2025. Establishing a state-level reporting system is a major milestone in strengthening institutional response frameworks and ensuring that cases of trafficking are systematically documented and addressed.•Facilitation of special sessions for school professionals on child trafficking - These sessions were deferred to align with the broader teacher training calendar, ensuring consistent messaging and reducing fragmentation in delivery. Once implemented, these sessions will play a pivotal role in enhancing the capacity of school personnel to detect, prevent, and respond to trafficking risks.•Orientation for school representatives on victim identification ‘Standard Operating Procedures’ (SOPs) - Postponed ensuring consistency with national SOPs currently under review by NAPTIP. Aligning with national standards is critical for institutional coherence and for fostering trust between schools, communities, and statutory authorities.Each of these deferred activities plays an essential role in achieving the project’s long-term objectives. They collectively strengthen the project’s pillars of community mobilisation, institutional capacity, and systems development for trafficking prevention and response. By strategically integrating them into the 2025 work plan, the STEAP team is committed to delivering them with renewed focus, stronger coordination mechanisms, and deeper stakeholder engagement. These efforts will ensure not only the achievement of intended outcomes but also the sustainability and scalability of project interventions beyond the current cycle. CHALLENGES AND MITIGATION STEAP implementation challenges during the reporting periodDuring the reporting period, the STEAP project team encountered several operational and contextual challenges that affected the pace and sequencing of implementation across the five target states. A summary of the key constraints and how the project team proactively responded is thus highlighted below:a) Insecurity in Benue and Enugu states - The volatile security situation in parts of Benue and Enugu—primarily due to incidents linked to herdsmen attacks and IPOB activity posed significant risks to safe access and implementation. Some communities where schools were originally selected experienced persistent unrest, forcing the project to adjust plans.Mitigation: The project team conducted joint security assessments with local partners and adapted the implementation plan accordingly. This included rerouting travel plans, temporarily replacing schools in high-risk areas with safer alternatives, and liaising with community leaders to ensure beneficiary and staff safety.b) Delay in project vehicle delivery - The late delivery of official project vehicles delayed movement and field logistics, especially in Q1–Q3 2024, slowing implementation of planned .Resolution: Vehicles were delivered to the Abuja office on 10 December 2024, and full mobility has since been restored for improved field operations in 2025.c) Change in NAPTIP leadership - The leadership transition at NAPTIP in August 2024 caused a temporary disruption in their subcontracted project roles, including delays in tool finalization and activity rollout.Mitigation: The new Director-General was formally briefed on STEAP and NAPTIP’s deliverables. With the endorsement secured, NAPTIP resumed full implementation, including their support role in SOP development and school club inauguration and oversight.d) Political transition in Edo state - The governorship election and subsequent administrative turnover in Edo state led to decreased participation from previously engaged officials. Key government contacts (e.g., Commissioners, Permanent secretaries) were reassigned or exited office, requiring fresh engagement.Mitigation: Plans are in place to formally re-engage the new political leadership in Q1 2025 through advocacy visits and alignment meetings to secure renewed commitment and ownership.e) Geographical distance and travel constraints - The geographic spread of the five target states (Benue, Delta, Edo, Enugu, Ogun) created logistical complexity and added transit time for inter-state activities.Mitigation: To reduce fatigue and maximize efficiency, the project team grouped geographically closer states for back-to-back activities and used regional clusters when planning school-level engagements and training events.Lessons Learnt During the reporting period, the STEAP project generated several important lessons that will shape ongoing implementation and inform future programming in similar contexts:•Community leadership is a Game-Changer - Engaging traditional, religious, and community leaders from the outset proved highly effective in gaining community trust and reducing cultural resistance to sensitive issues such as trafficking, sextortion, and ritual exploitation. For example, in Edo State, the vocal stance of the Oba of Benin against trafficking practices significantly contributed to local acceptance and cooperation.Lesson: Sustained engagement with influential local leaders enhances legitimacy, reduces pushback, and strengthens grassroots prevention mechanisms.•Insecurity requires agile programming - Security risks in Benue and Enugu highlighted the importance of flexible programming. Some pre-selected schools had to be changed due to community displacement and threats of violence.Lesson: Conflict-sensitive programming with alternative implementation routes and pre-identified backup sites is essential in volatile regions.•Curriculum ownership is strengthened by involvement - The ToT with 85 tutors across 38 institutions demonstrated that involving educators in curriculum delivery planning increases buy in and ensures sustainability. Tutors who co-created step-down plans showed higher commitment to rollout.Lesson: Curriculum dissemination is more impactful when educators are involved in the delivery strategy.•Low awareness does not mean low risk – In Ogun low awareness of trafficking in human beings (THB) among students was found alongside several underlying vulnerabilities. This highlights that low awareness often correlates with higher risk and reinforces the need to consider both awareness levels and socio-economic risk indicators when selecting target schools and tailoring interventions. Lesson: Effective targeting of schools for anti-trafficking interventions must therefore be informed by both awareness levels and socio-economic risk factors to ensure that support reaches the most at-risk populations.•Gendered trafficking trends demand tailored messaging - Baseline findings revealed that boys are increasingly being recruited for cybercrime or labour trafficking while girls face sexual exploitation, egg harvesting, and domestic servitude. Lesson: One-size-fits-all IEC campaigns are insufficient gender- and age-responsive materials are crucial for accurate risk communication.•PTA/SBMC structures are underutilized but promising - Across the five states, PTAs and SBMCs expressed willingness to engage in anti-trafficking awareness but lacked direction and tools. Lesson: These structures offer a ready-made platform for THB prevention if they are capacitated and formally linked to school clubs and referral systems.•Distance and administrative boundaries require strategic planning - Travel and coordination across five geographically dispersed states stretched team capacity and resources.Lesson: Regional clustering of activities and rotating staff teams based on location can enhance cost-efficiency and reduce fatigue.•Policy shifts require proactive political engagement - Leadership changes at NAPTIP and in Edo State affected activity continuity. Quick realignment efforts helped restore momentum. Lesson: Political transitions should be anticipated as a project risk and managed through structured onboarding briefings, documentation handovers, and formal advocacy visits.STRATEGIC NEXT STEPS AND PRIORITY ACTIONS (2025)1. Technical review and refinement of the STEAP Results and Indicators matrixA priority in early 2025 will be the technical review of the STEAP Results and Indicators Matrix approved in November 2023. This review will incorporate learning from Year 1 implementation, stakeholder feedback, and emerging field realities and will enhance the project’s ability to monitor results in real-time and to adaptively manage interventions for greater impact.The review will focus on:•Ensuring indicators are SMART, contextually relevant, and disaggregated appropriately (e.g., by age, gender, geography).•Refining output and outcome definitions for clarity, measurability, and attribution.•Improving data collection tools and timelines to better capture changes in knowledge, attitudes, and behaviours.•Aligning with national and state-level monitoring frameworks to promote harmonized reporting and reduce duplication.2. Inauguration and strengthening of ‘School Anti-Trafficking Vanguard Clubs’To foster sustained student engagement and peer-led advocacy, the project will inaugurate Anti-Trafficking Vanguard Clubs in selected schools across the five states. These clubs will serve as critical platforms for building student agency and school-based prevention culture.Key activities will include:•Formal club inauguration ceremonies in collaboration with school authorities and State Ministries of Education.•Structured training for student leaders and teacher facilitators on THB issues, child rights, and safe reporting.•Distribution of standardised toolkits to guide club activities, including discussion guides, posters, and peer education materials.3. Rollout of CSO-led community outreach and awareness campaignsFollowing the onboarding of CSOs, a major outreach campaign will be launched targeting parents, caregivers, traditional leaders, and local influencers. The campaign will be evaluated for its effectiveness in shifting awareness and triggering protective behaviours at the community level.This campaign will:•Use culturally appropriate messages to challenge norms that enable trafficking.•Leverage radio, community theatre, and local events to increase reach and resonance.•Promote available reporting channels and referral services.4. Operationalization of reporting lines and referral pathwaysThe project will work with NAPTIP, State Taskforces, and education authorities to finalize and disseminate clear, practical referral mechanisms for trafficking-related cases. This action is vital for closing the loop between identification and protection and ensuring timely effective support for affected children.This includes:•Mapping existing services and protection actors in each state.•Developing school-level reporting protocols aligned with national SOPs.•Training school focal points and SBMC members on how to recognize, report, and respond to potential trafficking cases.5. Strengthening of SBMCs and continued training for school personnelTo deepen institutional capacity at the school and community levels, as well as institutionalising a dual approach that will ensure stronger local governance and protection capacity within the school system, the project will:•Conduct targeted training for SBMCs based on the results of their 2025 assessment.•Provide refresher training for headteachers, classroom teachers, and school administrators on child safeguarding, trafficking risk factors, and response protocols.6. Funding and implementation of ‘School Improvement Projects’.Using data from school priorities identified in collaboration with SBMCs, STEAP will support the implementation of small-scale school improvement initiatives, and these investments will serve as tangible demonstrations of community-school collaboration and incentivize continued SBMC engagement thus aimed at:•Creating safer and more engaging learning environments (e.g., improved lighting, fencing, toilets, clean water, safe spaces for girls).•Reinforcing the protective role of schools against trafficking.7. Strengthening partnerships and promoting sustainabilityTo institutionalize project achievements and foster long-term sustainability, strategic collaboration is critical to embedding project practices within government systems and community structures. STEAP will:•Formalize partnerships with State Ministries of Education, Women Affairs, and Justice, as well as NAPTIP and other Taskforce members.•Establish regular coordination platforms at state level to harmonize anti-trafficking efforts.•Facilitate joint planning and monitoring visits to encourage government co-ownership and continuity beyond the project lifecycle.DONOR RECOGNITIONThe STEAP project extends its heartfelt appreciation to the Government of the Netherlands for its invaluable support and trusted partnership. This collaboration has been instrumental in driving forward efforts to prevent child trafficking and strengthen protective systems in schools and communities across the five target states in Nigeria. The Netherlands’ unwavering commitment to human rights, child protection, and community empowerment has enabled the project to take a holistic, evidence-based approach one that places local ownership, sustainability, and long-term impact at its core.ICMPD is proud to work alongside partners like the Government of the Netherlands, whose voluntary support makes this work possible. Their contribution has not only advanced the project’s goals but also reinforced Nigeria’s broader efforts to build a society free from trafficking. The STEAP team is deeply grateful for the Netherlands’ strategic vision, flexibility, and continued support, which is making a real difference in the lives of vulnerable children and the communities that protect them.
